analysis.one_liner: Bans doctors from referring patients to labs, imaging centers, and clinics they own, for all payers.
analysis.headline: The bill never came up for a vote in the House; a narrower version of its physician referral-ban expansion was enacted later in 1993 through the budget reconciliation law.
analysis.plain_summary: Under Medicare rules already on the books, doctors cannot send patients to clinical labs they have a financial stake in. This bill would broaden that ban in two big ways: it would cover many more services — physical therapy, MRI and CT scans, radiation therapy, medical equipment, prescription drugs, ambulances, home infusion, occupational therapy, and hospital care — and it would apply the ban to every payer, not just Medicare and Medicaid, so privately insured patients get the same protection. It also tightens the rules on the remaining exceptions, requiring that leases and other payments between doctors and providers be set at fair market value and not tied to the volume of referrals a doctor generates.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and taxpayers. When doctors own the lab, the imaging center, or the therapy clinic they refer to, they profit from ordering more care. Extending the ban beyond Medicare means privately insured patients, whose premiums rise when unnecessary services are billed, are protected too; the ban applies whenever 'a charge is imposed' for a designated health service [S3]. Medicare and other federal and state health programs also benefit, because the bill bars payment for claims submitted in violation of the referral ban [S3]. Hospitals also stand to gain, since referrals for labs and imaging that once flowed to physician-owned facilities would flow to hospitals instead.

how_it_helps.text: Expands the ban on physician self-referral from clinical lab services to eleven categories of 'designated health services,' including physical and occupational therapy, radiology (MRI, CT scans, ultrasound), radiation therapy, durable medical equipment, outpatient prescription drugs, ambulance services, home infusion therapy, and inpatient and outpatient hospital services [S3].

Extends the referral ban to all payers, not just Medicare: it applies whenever a charge is imposed for the service, and bars payment by Medicare, other federal health programs, state health care programs, and third-party payers for claims submitted in violation of the ban [S3].

Tightens the exceptions that remain: office-space and equipment leases must be set in advance at fair market value and cannot be determined by the volume or value of referrals, and compensation arrangements must be 'commercially reasonable even if no referrals were made' [S3].

Adds targeted safeguards for legitimate arrangements — a rural-provider exception so rural patients do not lose access to care, plus narrow exceptions for bona fide employment, consultative second opinions, pathology, and faculty practice plans — while requiring Secretary-level regulation 'to protect against program or patient abuse' [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Physicians who own stakes in clinical labs, imaging centers, physical therapy clinics, medical-equipment suppliers, ambulance companies, and similar businesses, who would lose the ability to profit from referring patients to their own ventures. Their businesses would also bear compliance costs: written leases, fair-market-value pricing, and documentation that payments are not tied to referral volume.
analysis.who_pays_short: Physicians with stakes in referral businesses

drawbacks.text: The bill itself acknowledges an access concern: it creates a rural-provider exception so that people in rural areas do not lose services when the only nearby provider has a physician financial relationship [S3].

Even a conflict-of-interest ban draws lines by judgment, and this one leaves physician group practices largely able to furnish ancillary services in-house under the group-practice provisions — meaning many ownership arrangements would survive the ban [S3].

Strict fair-market-value and no-referral-influence tests for every lease and compensation arrangement add real compliance paperwork for honest providers, and the bill's own exception list (consultations, pathology, phlebotomy, employer health services) shows how many arrangements Congress judged too useful to prohibit outright [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is worth weighing honestly. Ownership referrals were documented drivers of overuse in lab and imaging services, and extending the ban to private payers closes a real gap — privately insured patients pay for unnecessary scans and therapy through premiums. The costs are real but limited: physician-owners lose a profit stream, honest providers face compliance paperwork, and rural-access concerns are addressed with an exception rather than ignored. The main design weakness is the survival of the group-practice carve-out, which the enacted version of this idea later turned into a large loophole. Overall, a patient-protection bill with manageable, acknowledged costs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill never got a vote of its own — after subcommittee hearings in April 1993, the record simply notes it was folded into H.R. 2264, the 1993 budget reconciliation bill, and the version of the referral-ban expansion that became law (known as Stark II) covered more services but dropped this bill's push to apply the ban to all payers and kept the ban limited to Medicare and Medicaid.

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Stark of California introduced the bill on January 5, 1993; it was referred jointly to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees, and to their health subcommittees [S5][S1].
Rep. Sander Levin of Michigan was added as an additional sponsor on April 1, 1993, and six House members in total cosponsored the bill — five Democrats and one Republican [S4].
A House subcommittee held hearings on the bill on April 20, 1993, but neither committee ever reported it to the full House, and no floor vote ever took place [S5].
On August 10, 1993, the action history notes 'See H.R. 2264' — the standard record convention meaning the bill's substance was taken up through that bill, the 1993 budget reconciliation measure [S5].

What became law through that vehicle (the expansion known as Stark II) covered more designated health services but did not include this bill's extension of the ban to all payers, and it preserved a broad in-office exception for physician group practices; this is well-established public reporting not contained in the provided sources.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Physicians who own labs, imaging centers, and therapy clinics came out ahead relative to the bill as written: the enacted version left ownership of ancillary services largely intact and limited the ban to Medicare and Medicaid, while still locking in a statutory framework they can operate within.

against.name: Physician-owned laboratories, imaging centers, and ancillary-service businesses
against.what_they_did: The expansion of the self-referral ban to more services faced sustained resistance from physician investors in these facilities, and the version ultimately enacted left the all-payers extension out and preserved the in-office exception.

sides.party_line_note: All six cosponsors were House members — five Democrats and one Republican — so the sponsorship was overwhelmingly, though not entirely, Democratic; no recorded votes exist to measure wider support.

industries.industry: Physician-owned medical facilities (clinical labs, imaging centers, therapy clinics, medical-equipment and ambulance companies)
industries.note: The bill would prohibit physicians from referring patients — for Medicare, Medicaid, private insurance, or any other payer — to businesses they have a financial stake in, and would require that any remaining leases and payments be priced at fair market value independent of referral volume. These businesses profit from the referral stream the bill cuts off, so their gain historically came at patients' and payers' expense.

Referrals for lab work, imaging, and therapy that once flowed to physician-owned facilities would instead flow to hospitals, including psychiatric and rehabilitation hospitals, which the bill explicitly brings under the designated-services ban structure. Hospital care for Medicare patients would be the lawful channel.

Even as it tightens the ban, the bill maintains and clarifies the group-practice carve-out: services billed in the group's name under a group billing number, and hospital-group lab arrangements meeting strict grandfathering and fair-market-value tests, remain permissible. Group practice remains the lawful route for in-house ancillary services.

Standalone labs lose physician-owner referrals but gain a market protected from ownership-based competition, and the bill keeps narrow exceptions for physician-paid lab services and certain hospital-group lab arrangements predating 1989.
